Hi jack, I'm sure it's been covered in *some* discussion but that's all a bit spread out, so no blame. It should probably be answered again in RFC 163 or a new one.

For some services it may make sense for the traditional NixOS service to be a wrapper that installs the right modular service that does the same thing.
For things like desktop environments or very "global" ones like nscd it makes sense to keep them as they are, although for instance nscd could exist as both, where the traditional one configures the whole system, and the modular one only runs a daemon that happens to be nscd.

dawn's recent episode touches on the step from traditional systemd (like nixos now) to distributed scheduling. on that topic, it occurred to me that the primary info needed to run things in k8s (as per DetSys's nix-to-kubernetes repo) seems argv, info which portable services already expose.

that actually reminds me - tho we may not have examples yet, iirc portable services also offered associating multiple services with a package. i guess that could for one be used to facilitate running different services from the same package in a distributed fashion. i maybe wonder now though, what use-cases for separate services did we already have in mind so far?

most NixOS services produce one systemd service, but some consist of multiple (often just `<something>-init.service`, but sometimes more interesting), and some services, like gitlab, are compositions of multiple services and external infrastructure
configuring multiple hosts at once is not part of modular services as currently framed, but something could be built around it to enable that kind of thing
it would benefit from having a single way to specify a service, even if one runs on k8s and another on NixOS

As I see it, modular services provide a single API between service managers (e.g. NixOS/systemd) and services. Configuring when and where services run isn't part of that single API but could be in something implementing modular services integration just like the one in NixOS. IIRC the service manager integration can also provide extra APIs/options just like `systemd.*` in the NixOS one.

`system.services.*` in NixOS makes sure that the service will basically be started when the NixOS system boots, but other modules can provide different ways of starting modules. There currently isn't a good way to specify dependencies between services but the [Contracts RFC](https://github.com/NixOS/rfcs/pull/189) should solve that

A modular service is loaded into a submodule, which means it's a separate module evaluation that can reference basically anything, even in `imports`. So that's another way to solve that same problem. Basically you can always import from "parents" whether that's the lexical scope, any file, or just following `submodule` in the other direction (e.g. the NixOS configuration root / empty option path). Or `specialArgs`, that's *almost* the lexical scope in my view.
So when you do nested services, you can have an option in your parent service that controls whether certain sub-services exist, what's imported into them, etc.

don't jump to conclusions and judge finit though... it is actually superior to systemd (from a nixos perspective) in this regard... years ago the nixos systemd team actually talked about implementing something very similar to what finit does out of the box

I think ultimately splitting a packaging and configuration implementation across repositories is asking for occasional trouble when version mismatches happen. These don't even have to be because of "breaking" changes. If the configuration part gets ahead of the package, it may insert unknown settings and cause the configuration to fail.
Similarly, the division of labor between the Nixpkgs module and the finix module would cause similar friction. This would make building the abstractions we want *harder* in practice.

so i feel like at the core of this repo question (experimenting with modular services in a nixpkgs fork vs in a new repo taking nixpkgs as dep) may be these perspectives on modular services as this new features needing services and users to get contributor/user balls rolling, vs seeing it as this experimental refactor that short-term doesn't so much unlock much interesting new user-facing functionality just yet, and mostly still just needs for a small team to have a quick and safe way to iterate on it

i must admit there is a grain of truth in a notion of new features, in the sense we could support more portable environments such as devenv - tho i would argue that our expressiveness is still just far from the point of being useful over existing offers already just yet
as such, my substitute for 'UX test' would be just "does the refactor result in identical drvs" - i.e. in practice it's just about drying up a sample of service implementations across environments

my reasoning: 'scaling' to services today just means scaling today's pain of writing a service (the size of the per-environment escape hatch that today just means manually writing your entire service for each environment after all) - I would suggest that to only so much consider that worthwhile once we manage to _significantly_ limit that pain.
